title: Catch-All (Optional Parameter) Queries
description: A '(@p IS NULL OR col=@p)' catch-all gets one bad plan for every case; OPTION(RECOMPILE) folds the unused branches into a seek. Why it matters: "search with optional filters" is one of the most commonly built features in business applications, and the naive catch-all pattern is a well-known way to tank performance for every caller at once.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine a search form with five optional filters — name, status, region, date range, category — where a user can fill in any combination of them, including none at all. Behind the scenes, it's tempting to write one single query that handles every possible combination at once, using a pattern like "only apply this filter if a value was actually provided." This lesson is about why that seemingly elegant, one-size-fits-all approach quietly produces a bad execution plan almost every single time it runs.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** This lesson is about the "catch-all query" pattern — typically written as something like `WHERE (@Status IS NULL OR Status = @Status) AND (@Region IS NULL OR Region = @Region)`, repeated for every optional filter — which is a very natural way to express "apply this condition only if the caller actually supplied a value for it," using a single reusable piece of SQL instead of building a different query for every possible combination of filters.

**Why this happens in real databases.** "Search with optional filters" is one of the most common query shapes in real business applications — practically every list screen, admin panel, and search page needs to let users filter by whichever combination of fields they care about, leaving the rest blank. Writing one catch-all query to cover every combination, rather than building a different query per possible combination, is the obvious and natural approach for a developer to reach for, and it does produce correct results in every case. The problem isn't correctness — it's that the optimizer has to compile *one single plan* for a query whose actual selectivity varies enormously depending on which parameters happen to be filled in on any given call.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** When SQL Server compiles this query, it has to pick one plan that will be reused (from cache) across every future call, regardless of which specific parameters are actually supplied at that future point. But the query's real-world behavior varies wildly: a call where only `@Status` is filled in might match a huge portion of the table, while a call where `@Status`, `@Region`, and `@Category` are all filled in together might match only a handful of rows — and a call where nothing is filled in should just return everything. The optimizer, at compile time, doesn't know which of these situations will actually occur on any given execution; it can only build one plan, based on whatever assumptions it makes about the typical case (often falling back to a generic, unhelpful estimate very similar to the parameter-sniffing problem seen elsewhere in this course). Whatever single plan it settles on, that same plan then gets reused, from cache, for every subsequent call — including calls whose actual selectivity is nothing like what the compiled plan assumed. A plan optimized for "assume most parameters are supplied and narrow things down a lot" performs badly on a call that leaves everything blank; a plan optimized for "assume broad, unfiltered access" performs badly on a call that supplies every filter and should have matched only a few rows.

**Why this matters in production.** This is one of the most common query patterns in real applications with any kind of flexible search or filter UI, and it's also one of the most reliable sources of "this report is fast for some users and painfully slow for others," purely depending on which combination of filters each user happens to select — with no code bug involved at all, just one compiled plan being a poor fit for the wide range of actual runtime scenarios it's asked to handle. This is exactly the kind of problem that's easy to miss in testing, because a developer testing with one particular combination of filters will only ever see the one plan behavior that matches their own test data and parameter choices, never the full range of behavior real users will trigger.

The fix demonstrated in this lesson is the same tool used for local-variable parameter sniffing: `OPTION (RECOMPILE)`. Applied to a catch-all query, it does something particularly powerful — because SQL Server recompiles fresh for every execution with the actual current parameter values in hand, and because a parameter that's `NULL` makes its corresponding `(@p IS NULL OR col = @p)` branch trivially always-true, the optimizer can effectively simplify away the filters that weren't actually used on this call and build a plan tailored specifically to the filters that were, for each individual execution. The cost is recompiling every time (a real trade-off, discussed elsewhere in this course), but the payoff is that every call gets a plan actually shaped for its own real selectivity, instead of every call sharing one generic compromise plan that's well-suited to none of them.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below runs the same catch-all query with different combinations of filters left blank or filled in, and shows you the same cached plan being reused regardless — performing well for some combinations and poorly for others. After adding `OPTION (RECOMPILE)`, re-run each combination and watch every single call get its own plan, tailored specifically to whichever filters were actually supplied that time, with unused `IS NULL` branches effectively optimized away for that execution.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** `OPTION (RECOMPILE)` isn't the only way to handle catch-all queries — an alternative, sometimes used when recompiling every call is too expensive, is to build the query dynamically in application code or via dynamic SQL, including in the `WHERE` clause only the conditions that actually have a value supplied, so the compiled plan for any given call only ever contains the filters that are genuinely active. That approach avoids recompilation entirely but adds the complexity (and injection-safety considerations) of building SQL text dynamically, which is why `OPTION (RECOMPILE)` is usually the simpler starting point unless recompilation cost specifically becomes a measured problem.

It's worth remembering that this same catch-all pattern shows up under other names too — "search screens," "dynamic filters," "advanced search" — but the underlying compiled-plan mismatch problem, and the `OPTION (RECOMPILE)` fix, is identical regardless of what the feature is actually called in the application.

## Scenario
A search screen lets the user optionally filter by customer. The classic "catch-all" pattern handles the optional filter in one query:

```sql
WHERE (@CustomerId IS NULL OR CustomerId = @CustomerId)
```

When `@CustomerId IS NULL` it should return everything; otherwise just that customer. But even when a value **is** supplied, the query scans the whole table.

## Why it's slow
SQL Server compiles **one** plan and caches it for reuse across all future values — including `@CustomerId IS NULL` (match everything). A plan that must be correct for the match-all case can't rely on seeking `CustomerId`, so the optimizer picks a **scan** that is safe for every value. The runtime value of `@CustomerId` doesn't change the cached plan.

## The fix
`OPTION (RECOMPILE)` tells SQL Server to recompile the statement **on each execution using the actual parameter value**. With `@CustomerId = 42`, the optimizer can prove the `@CustomerId IS NULL` branch is false, simplify the predicate to `CustomerId = 42`, and **seek** the index. The cost is a compile per execution — usually a fine trade for an otherwise unavoidable scan. (Building the statement as **dynamic SQL** with only the needed predicates is the other common fix.)

## Not the same as parameter sniffing
A separate lesson covers a *local variable* causing a cardinality **under-estimate**. Here the plan shape itself is forced wide by the `OR`-with-`NULL`; `RECOMPILE` fixes it by removing the branch at compile time.
hints: The (@p IS NULL OR col=@p) shape forces one plan that must also serve the match-all (@p IS NULL) case — a scan.
The runtime value can't change a cached plan. You need the optimizer to see the actual value at compile time.
Add OPTION (RECOMPILE) so the @CustomerId IS NULL branch is simplified away and CustomerId = @CustomerId can seek.
